questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Area of an Unbounded Region
questions.problem: Find the total area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y=3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}$ and the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x
$$

We start by calculating the first of these integrals:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x
$$

We calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u={x}^{3}$,  then $\text{d}u=3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.$ Hence, the antiderivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={e}^{u}+C \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{({e}^{{x}^{3}})|}_{a}^{0} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{0}-{e}^{{a}^{3}}) \\  & =1-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{x}^{2}{e}^{-|x{|}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral With Unbounded Limits
questions.worked_solution:
We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let  $u={x}^{2}$,  then $\text{d}u=2x\text{d}x.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{9+{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{u}{3}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the first of the improper integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{2x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{(\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})|}_{a}^{0} \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{{0}^{2}}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{{a}^{2}}{3}) \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(0-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{{a}^{2}}{3}) \\  & =0-\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **odd** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x=\frac{\pi }{6}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{x}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the total area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y=|x|{e}^{-{x}^{2}}$ and the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }|x|{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }|x|{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}|x|{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }|x|{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We start by calculating the first of these integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}|x|{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=-{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let  $u=-{x}^{2}$,  then $\text{d}u=-2x\text{d}x.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{u}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-{x}^{2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}|x|{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }({-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-{x}^{2}}|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{0}-{e}^{-{a}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $|x|{e}^{-{x}^{2}}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }|x|{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }|x|{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}|x|{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }|x|{e}^{-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral With Unbounded Limits
questions.worked_solution:
We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x
$$

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let  $u=3+{x}^{2}$,  then $\text{d}u=2x\text{d}x.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{u})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2(3+{x}^{2})}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the first of the improper integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{(-\frac{1}{2(3+{x}^{2})})|}_{a}^{0} \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{2(3+0)}-\frac{1}{2(3+{a}^{2})}) \\  & =-(\frac{1}{6}-0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **odd** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{x}{{(3+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Improper Integral With Unbounded Limits
questions.worked_solution:
We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{3}{9+2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3}{9+2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{9+2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3}{9+2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{3}{9+2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{(\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }({\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}x}{3})|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\operatorname{arctan}⁡0-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{2}a}{3})] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot [0-(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{9+2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{\pi }{2\sqrt{2}}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{3}{9+2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{3}{9+2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{3}{9+2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\pi }{2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
